M09_sonicDNA.title: Sonic DNA (locked at brief approval)

Any deviation requires explicit user re-approval (the sonic-drift guard). Derived from M03_genre + M05_vocal + R12_production + M07_runtime at brief-approval time. M01_concept.value: Pyro Altar front person Cole Sterling looks back at his late-teen / early-20s years (roughly age 15 to 22) with adult eyes. The album is a loose collection of memory vignettes — each track a standalone fragment of those years, not a single chronological arc. The central emotional thread is the slow-realization question 'where did the time go?' — tenderness, not bitterness; looking back at youth with adult eyes, sometimes amused, sometimes wistful, but never cruel. The album is autobiographical in texture but fictional in detail: scenes are drawn from the feeling of those years, not documentary re-tellings. Held together by the Pyro Altar sonic identity (M03 grunge + FF melodic) and Cole's Velvet Revolver-style vocal (M05) — the same voice looking back at the same memories from the same band, not a different artist reflecting on a different life. Vignettes are loose but not random: each is a moment the band could actually play, not a stream-of-consciousness journal entry. M02 (12 tracks, ~46 min) and M07 (3:00–3:30 per track) still hold; the 12 vignettes each fit a single track-length shape, and the tight runtime discipline keeps the vignettes from sprawling.

values.M01_concept_rationale: Concept = nostalgia album, late-teen / early-20s years, loose vignettes, 'where did the time go?' tenderness. Built from three M01 sub-questions, all answered option A: (M01.1) timeframe = late teens / coming-of-age (15–22) — the era where the band form, the music takes over, the first shows, the first heartbreak, the 'don't know who I am yet' phase. (M01.2) central question = 'Where did the time go?' — the slow realization that youth is over, looking back with tenderness (option A from the 4 nostalgia themes). (M01.3) narrative scope = loose vignettes — no single arc, each track a standalone memory fragment (option A from the 4 scope options). Rethink rationale: the original M01 (locked 2026-08-02 ~19:50 UTC) was a Foo Fighters-style autobiographical recovery album about a broken ankle and 6-month physiotherapy arc. User pushed back on 2026-08-02 ~20:30 UTC: 'i want to change the album topic, this is so stupid. grunge album about phisiotherapy??' — clear signal that the recovery/P.T. framing was untenable. M01 rebuilt from scratch on the nostalgia direction (option 1 of 6 nostalgia directions offered). The 12-track / 3:00–3:30 runtime discipline (M02 and M07, both locked) was preserved as discipline constraints — loose vignettes don't need week-by-week logic, they just need 12 distinct moments. M04 references (FF In Your Honor, Nirvana In Utero) and M05 vocal (Velvet Revolver / Weiland) both still serve this concept: FF In Your Honor is explicitly a nostalgia record (the acoustic side), and Weiland's VR delivery is a high-register melodic-grit voice that can carry tenderness without losing edge. R09 title 'Learning to Walk' retained for now — works as a metaphor for navigating the early years, but flagged for user re-evaluation. Locked 2026-08-02.
values.M02_scope_rationale: Standard album — 12 tracks, ~46 min target. Originally framed as '2 tracks per month of recovery' under the v1 concept; re-derivation under v2 (nostalgia) is the same: 12 tracks = 12 distinct vignettes from the late-teen / early-20s years. Each vignette gets a single track. Loose vignettes without a single arc still need 12 anchor points — 12 is the right count for the spread of memories (first love, first show, the band form, the last summer, etc.). 12 tracks also gives room for the M03 grunge + FF melodic dual-mode: ~6 hard-rocking tracks (the big memories) and ~6 quieter/melodic tracks (the intimate ones). User picked option 1 of 3. Chosen 2026-08-02; concept re-derived 2026-08-02 ~20:35 UTC.
values.M03_genre: 90s grunge with Foo Fighters melodic hooks
values.M03_genre_rationale: Best of both — raw tone and weight of 90s grunge (Pearl Jam, Nirvana, AIC, STP, Soundgarden) with Foo Fighters' sing-along chorus structure and melodic hooks. The Foo Fighters are the post-grunge/melodic bridge that keeps the album accessible while the grunge backbone keeps it heavy. User picked option 3 of 3. Chosen 2026-08-02.

M04_references.what_for: melodic recovery + quiet-to-loud dynamic + introspective lyrical tone

values.M04_references_rationale: Two-ref classical setup. FF (In Your Honor) carries the introspection + melodic side — the album IS explicitly a nostalgia record, the acoustic-side tracks like 'Razor' and 'Cold Day in the Sun' are the canonical reference for tenderness-with-edge. Nirvana (In Utero) carries the raw + grunge-pain side — the angst of those years, the unrestrained teenage voice. Both anchors map cleanly to the M03 genre hybrid (FF melodic + grunge raw). Two refs chosen over three to avoid over-constraining the system. Re-derivation under v2 (nostalgia) retains both FF and Nirvana — FF In Your Honor is the strongest nostalgia reference in the M04 universe, Nirvana In Utero provides the raw teenage-voice counterweight. User delegated to agent (option 1 was the recommendation). Chosen 2026-08-02; concept re-derived 2026-08-02 ~20:35 UTC.

M05_vocal.approach: high-register melodic-grit belt with dynamic range
M05_vocal.texture: dry studio with light plate reverb; doubled lead on choruses
M05_vocal.pitch_note: slightly higher than typical rock vocal (tenor register, not baritone)
M05_vocal.chorus_dynamic: opens up to full belt with grit; soaring high notes on key phrases
M05_vocal.notes: Velvet Revolver (Weiland) is the bridge between FF melodic and Nirvana raw — high-register melodic-grit belt. Verses intimate/controlled, choruses open up to soaring belt with grit. Tenor register (higher than typical rock baritone).

values.M05_vocal_rationale: Velvet Revolver (Scott Weiland) is the perfect third anchor — literally the bridge between the M04 FF-melodic and Nirvana-raw refs. Weiland's voice is high-register, theatrical, melodic-grit, with wide dynamic range. Higher pitch than FF (Weiland was a tenor; Grohl is a baritone) which matches the user's request for 'higher pitch'. Dynamic range (intimate verses → soaring choruses) maps to the recovery arc. User explicit pick (not delegated). Chosen 2026-08-02.

M06_language.notes: English only, 100% of album. No language mixing. Standard for 90s grunge genre and all three M04 references (FF, Nirvana, VR — all American English-language rock bands).

values.M06_language_rationale: English only (100%) — default for English-language rock. Matches all 3 M04 references (FF, Nirvana, VR — all American English-language bands). Keeps the conceptual focus tight on the recovery arc without language-mixing distraction. User explicit pick (option 1). Chosen 2026-08-02.

M07_runtime.notes: Tight 3:00-3:30 range. Most In Utero tracks fit this (Pennyroyal Tea 3:31, All Apologies 3:51 — at upper end). Many FF tracks fit (Cold Day in the Sun 3:45 slightly over). The tight range maximizes single-friendliness and forces discipline. With 12 tracks × ~3:15 avg = ~39 min album total.

values.M07_runtime_rationale: Tight 3:00-3:30 per track — more 'single-friendly' than 'album-track' runtime. Classic grunge shape: most Nirvana In Utero tracks fall in this range (Pennyroyal Tea 3:31, All Apologies 3:51 — slightly over upper bound, but close). Many Foo Fighters tracks fit (Cold Day in the Sun 3:45 just over the bound). 12 tracks × ~3:15 avg = ~39 min album total — well below the M02 ~46 min target but acceptable for tight runtime. User explicit pick (option tightened beyond the 3 offered). Chosen 2026-08-02.
values.R09_title_rationale: Album title = 'Twenty-Two'. The upper bound of the era the album looks back at (age 15–22). Single-age, no metaphor overhead, ages itself honestly. Tells you exactly what the album is about — the years up to and including twenty-two. Re-derivation under v2 (nostalgia): the original 'Learning to Walk' (locked 2026-08-02 ~20:13 UTC) was a recovery/P.T. metaphor; under v2 nostalgia the title still works as 'navigating the early years' but the meaning shifted enough to warrant a re-pick. 'Twenty-Two' is the cleanest v2 title: FF used single-age/era single-words (Dove, One by One, 01020225) as working titles — same direct era anchor. Single-word single-number tracks well as a brand mark. Renumbered album (not album 1) — neutral on whether the band has more albums, fits a debut or pre-debut. Agent pick under user 'you decide the rest' directive. Locked 2026-08-02 ~20:40 UTC.

tracks.title: Razor
tracks.theme: First guitar — felt the strings bite my fingers for the first time. Age 15. The beginning of the band before there was a band.

tracks.title: Summer of 19
tracks.theme: The last normal summer. Garages, gas money, no one paying anything. Before we were anyone.

tracks.title: First Show
tracks.theme: The first show — empty room, played to 9 people, 4 of them friends. Terrifying. Best night of my life.

tracks.title: Her Car
tracks.theme: First love. The make-out songs we wrote. The song I wrote three weeks after she left.

tracks.title: Twenty-Two
tracks.theme: The title track. The day I turned 22 and realized I was older than half the songs I still loved.

tracks.title: Basement
tracks.theme: Where we actually lived. The room we never cleaned, the gear we never paid for, the songs we wrote at 3am.

tracks.title: Open Mic
tracks.theme: The opening-act years. Playing to rooms of 30. The night someone asked us to play one more.

tracks.title: Mama
tracks.theme: Mom. The one who never said stop. The one who came to every show even when it was bad.

tracks.title: Freeway
tracks.theme: The first tour. Driving all night. The night the van broke down in Wyoming at 4am.

tracks.title: The Dive
tracks.theme: The bar where everything actually started. The stage that was 12 inches tall. The crowd that didn't know any of our songs.

tracks.title: Junior
tracks.theme: My younger self. The kid who picked up the guitar. What I'd say to him now.

tracks.title: Standing Still
tracks.theme: Closing track. The moment after the album ends — looking back at all of it and being okay. Slow, deliberate, a kind of resolution.

values.R10_tracklist_rationale: 12 nostalgia vignettes for 'Twenty-Two'. Each track is a standalone memory fragment from the age 15-22 era, no single arc. Tracks are ordered chronologically-feeling but loosely: Track 1 is the earliest memory (age 15, first guitar), Track 12 is 'now' looking back. Between, the order implies a progression but doesn't require it — you can listen in any order and each track still works. The tracklist mixes 6 hard-rocking tracks (the loud memories: First Show, Open Mic, Freeway, The Dive) with 6 quieter/intimate tracks (the soft memories: Her Car, Basement, Mama, Junior). The title track 'Twenty-Two' sits at Track 5 — the emotional midpoint, the moment of recognition. Closing track 'Standing Still' is named the same as the closing track of v1's recovery tracklist (conceived but never written in v1) — kept under v2 because the title works as a closing gesture for a look-back album: standing still, looking back, being okay. Track 1 'Razor' is named after the FF In Your Honor track (M04 reference) — the system anchor that opens the album. Title shape: mostly 1-2 words, some noun phrases (Her Car, First Show, The Dive). Genre-aware: titles that work as both grunge-raw and FF-melodic (no R&B vocabulary, no country vocabulary). Agent pick under user 'you decide the rest' directive. Locked 2026-08-02 ~20:42 UTC.

R11_motif.value: Recurring motif: the same 4-chord progression (G–C–D–Em in open G, the easiest chord shape Cole ever learned at age 15), but played differently each time it appears. Track 1 'Razor' introduces it as a clean electric arpeggio (the first guitar memory). Track 5 'Twenty-Two' plays it as full-band power chords (the realization). Track 9 'Freeway' plays it as a dirty 12-string (the van, the highway). Track 11 'Junior' plays it as solo acoustic (addressing the younger self). Track 12 'Standing Still' plays it as full-band with strings (the resolution). The progression G–C–D–Em is the album's spine — recognizable as the same emotional core, but aged and worn across the tracks. The listener doesn't need to notice this consciously; the album just feels like one continuous look-back.

values.R11_motif_rationale: Motif = recurring 4-chord progression (G–C–D–Em), played differently each time it appears. Re-derivation under v2 (nostalgia): the v1 recovery concept had a literal walking motif (per-step rhythm changes per track); v2 needed a v2-scale motif. The 4-chord motif is the musical equivalent of 'the same kid, older': the progression is the same, the sound is older. Why G–C–D–Em specifically: it's the most basic 4-chord shape in open G (a guitar's first-position), the kind of progression a 15-year-old learns first. Tying the album's musical spine to the literal first-chords Cole ever learned collapses the distance between the listener and the memory. The arrangement evolves (clean → distorted → acoustic → full-band + strings), but the harmonic content is constant. Genre-aware: G–C–D–Em sits inside both grunge-raw (it'll distort beautifully on the loud tracks) and FF-melodic (it'll sound anthemic with the right vocal). Agent pick under user 'you decide the rest' directive. Locked 2026-08-02 ~20:45 UTC.
values.R12_production_rationale: Production = hybrid. Re-derivation under v2 (nostalgia): the v1 recovery concept had been leaning full-band (per the v1 flag) but v2 nostalgia benefits from FF In Your Honor's two-disc split — disc 1 full-band (the loud tracks: First Show, Freeway, The Dive, Open Mic, Standing Still), disc 2 / the quieter tracks stripped (Razor, Her Car, Basement, Mama, Junior). The hybrid shape mirrors the M02 6-loud / 6-quiet split without forcing the album into a single sonic mode. Matches M03 (grunge + FF melodic) — grunge lives on the loud tracks, FF melodic lives on the quiet ones. Matches the M04 FF In Your Honor reference (which IS this hybrid). Matches the M05 V/R vocal (Weiland's voice works on both modes). Production-of-record hint: large-room drums on the loud tracks ('the arena we wished we had at age 19'), close-mic'd acoustic and room tone on the quiet tracks ('the basement where we actually played'). Genre-aware: 'cinematic' was tempting but the vignette format doesn't want score-like orchestration; 'electronic' would fight the vintage tone; 'full-band' alone ignores the quiet half; 'stripped' alone ignores the loud half. Hybrid is the only honest choice. Agent pick under user 'you decide the rest' directive. Locked 2026-08-02 ~20:46 UTC.
values.R13_lyricalSource_rationale: Lyrical source = co-write. The user is providing the memoir (the memories from the 15-22 era); the agent is providing the lyric shape (the formal craft — meter, rhyme, structure, hook placement). This is the right division because the user has the memories only they have, but the agent has the lyric-tool experience (writing the structure tags [Verse]/[Chorus]/[Bridge] correctly for the CLI, balancing the Velvet-Revolver vocal range, hitting the 3:00-3:30 runtime envelope). NOT 'user-writes' because the user has not asked to write the lyrics themselves — they're driving the brief, not the lyrics. NOT 'agent-writes' because the album is autobiographical in texture (per M01), and the agent's job is to translate the user's memories into lyric shape, not to invent them. Workflow: at each track, the user provides the memory beat (e.g., 'make-out songs we wrote') and the agent drafts the lyric. The user reviews and either accepts, edits, or requests a re-draft. Co-write is also the most realistic MMX-music-aligned workflow: the CLI's --lyrics-optimizer runs on the user-provided lyric text, but the user can also pass a lyric file (--lyrics-file), and the agent hands the file to mmx. Agent pick under user 'you decide the rest' directive. Locked 2026-08-02 ~20:47 UTC.
values.R14_distribution_rationale: Distribution = just-for-me (default). The album is a personal nostalgia project — the user is the listener, not a public audience. This is the conservative default for a first-time album-studio walkthrough. Upgrading to 'routenote-free' (free distribution to limited DSPs like SoundCloud/YouTube Music) or 'full-dsp' (paid RouteNote annual to Spotify/Apple Music/Amazon/etc) is a future decision the user can make after the album exists and they've heard it. The 'just-for-me' default also keeps the focus on the music generation pipeline (M01-M13) rather than the marketing / distribution pipeline (R14 + cover art + press). Default = the schema's default value. Agent pick under user 'you decide the rest' directive. Locked 2026-08-02 ~20:48 UTC.
values.R15_loudnessTarget_rationale: Loudness target = spotify (default, -14 LUFS / true-peak -1 dB). Per the schema this is the streaming default. The album is 'just-for-me' (R14) so technically the loudness doesn't need to match any platform, but locking to -14 LUFS keeps the master stage honest (the finalize-album.py master stage reads this value) and means if the user upgrades distribution to routenote-free or full-dsp later, the album already meets the Spotify target. Default = the schema's default value. Agent pick under user 'you decide the rest' directive. Locked 2026-08-02 ~20:48 UTC.
values.R16_sequencePacing_rationale: Sequence pacing = standard-pause (3-4s between tracks, per the schema). The vignettes are loose but independent — each track is a standalone memory fragment, so a small breath between tracks lets each memory settle before the next begins. Continuous-flow (<1s gap, bleeds between tracks) would suggest the album is a single piece — wrong for vignettes. Short-pause (1-2s) is borderline but felt too tight for the emotional weight. Long-pause (5-7s) would feel like a compilation or a greatest-hits. Concept-pause (variable per-track, set by the brief) would be excess for an album that's already 12 distinct vignettes — the variability would be noise. Standard-pause matches the M07 3:00-3:30 runtime envelope (tight tracks need normal gaps, not zero gaps). Default = the schema's default value. Agent pick under user 'you decide the rest' directive. Locked 2026-08-02 ~20:49 UTC.
